questions.title: A flywheel, a hanging mass, and a brake
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.4 Rigid body mechanics (AHL): torque, moment of inertia of a disc, torque = I x angular acceleration, rotational kinetic energy
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: The string tension is not the weight of the hanging mass, so the acceleration has to be found by solving the linear and rotational equations simultaneously; the same tension then carries into the energy check, and the final stage switches from dynamics to rotational work with the string no longer driving anything.

questions.question: A uniform solid disc of mass $M=2.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R=0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ is mounted on a fixed horizontal axle. A light string is wound round the rim, does not slip, and hangs vertically with a mass $m=0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ attached to its free end. The disc is released from rest and the mass falls a distance $h=0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ before it reaches the floor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the acceleration of the falling mass is $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+M/2}$ and calculate its value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string while the mass is falling, and explain why it is less than the weight of the mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the speed of the mass as it reaches the floor, and verify your answer by comparing the loss of gravitational potential energy with the total kinetic energy gained.

parts.label: d
parts.text: After the mass lands the string goes slack. A brake then applies a constant torque of $0.24\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ about the axle. Calculate the number of complete revolutions the disc makes before it stops.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Let $T$ be the string tension and $a$ the acceleration of the mass; the string does not slip, so the angular acceleration of the disc is $\alpha=a/R$. **(M1)**

For the hanging mass: $mg-T=ma$ **(M1)**

For the disc, torque $\tau=TR$ and moment of inertia $I=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}$, so $TR=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{R}=\dfrac{1}{2}MRa$, giving $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma$. **(M1)(A1)**

Substituting: $mg-\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=ma$, so $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+\dfrac{M}{2}}$. **(AG)**

Numerically $a=\dfrac{0.80\times 9.81}{0.80+1.2}=\dfrac{7.848}{2.0}=3.92\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. **(A1)**

**(b)** $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.4\times 3.924=4.71\ \mathrm{N}$. **(M1)(A1)**

The weight of the mass is $mg=0.80\times 9.81=7.85\ \mathrm{N}$, so $T<mg$. **(A1)** The tension is less than the weight because the mass is accelerating downwards: the resultant downward force $mg-T$ is what supplies its acceleration, and if $T$ equalled $mg$ the mass would not accelerate at all. Equivalently, the tension is the torque that must be provided to give the disc its angular acceleration, and that comes at the cost of part of the weight.

**(c)** $v^{2}=2ah=2\times 3.924\times 0.90=7.063$, so $v=2.66\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(M1)(A1)**

Energy check: loss of potential energy $=mgh=0.80\times 9.81\times 0.90=7.06\ \mathrm{J}$. **(M1)**

The angular speed of the disc is $\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}=\dfrac{2.6577}{0.35}=7.59\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $I=\dfrac{1}{2}(2.4)(0.35)^{2}=0.1470\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}$, so the rotational kinetic energy is $\dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}(0.1470)(57.66)=4.24\ \mathrm{J}$.

Adding the translational kinetic energy of the mass, $\dfrac{1}{2}(0.80)(2.6577)^{2}=2.83\ \mathrm{J}$, gives $7.06\ \mathrm{J}$, which equals the loss of potential energy. **(A1)**

**(d)** At the moment the string goes slack the disc has $\omega=7.59\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and rotational kinetic energy $E_{k}=4.24\ \mathrm{J}$. **(M1)**

With a constant braking torque, the work done equals the change in rotational kinetic energy: $\tau\theta=E_{k}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{4.238}{0.24}=17.7\ \mathrm{rad}$. **(M1)(A1)**

$17.7\ \mathrm{rad}=\dfrac{17.66}{2\pi}=2.81$ revolutions, so the disc makes $2$ complete revolutions before stopping. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a): the **(AG)** requires both equations of motion to be stated before substitution. A candidate who writes $a=g$ — treating the disc as massless or the tension as zero — earns nothing beyond the first **(M1)**. Accept the use of $I=kMR^{2}$ with $k=1/2$ stated, and accept a solution by energy methods that differentiates an energy expression, provided the tension is still identified. Part (b): award the **(A1)** for the comparison only if a numerical or symbolic value of $mg$ is given. Part (c): the energy verification mark is independent of the kinematic calculation; a candidate whose kinematics slips but whose energy comparison is internally consistent still earns the final **(A1)**. Follow-through applies from (a). Part (d): the critical step is converting the rotational kinetic energy into an angle; a candidate who divides by $\tau$ but then forgets to convert radians to revolutions loses the last **(A1)** only. A common error is to use $E_{k}=\dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ with $\omega$ in revolutions per second; check units explicitly. Do not accept an answer of 2.81 revolutions without the conversion stated, and do not penalise a candidate who truncates to 2 with a correct reason.
questions.explanation:
The question is built around one misconception that survives right up to the final examination: that the falling mass accelerates at $g$. It cannot, because the string tension exerts a torque on a disc that has a finite moment of inertia, and that torque can only be produced if the tension differs from the weight. The disc therefore holds the mass back, and the acceleration depends on the ratio of the two masses. Part (b) makes the point explicit and demands the physical reason rather than the algebra.

The energy check in part (c) is not decoration. A student who computes $v=2.66\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from kinematics and then, in the energy check, assumes all the potential energy became translational kinetic energy will find $\sqrt{2gh}=4.20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and a total of $7.06\ \mathrm{J}$ from only $2.83\ \mathrm{J}$ of translational energy. The missing $4.24\ \mathrm{J}$ is the rotational kinetic energy of the flywheel, and locating it is the point of the question: for a solid disc with the string unwinding from the rim, roughly 60% of the energy ends up in the disc.

Part (d) changes regime deliberately. Once the string is slack there is no driving torque and no translational motion, so the problem becomes a rotational work calculation with a constant torque. The two common errors are to keep using the translational kinetic energy, or to use the angular speed in the wrong units. The answer is framed as complete revolutions to force the radians-to-revolutions conversion, which is where the mark is usually lost. A recurring error in part (a) is the wrong moment of inertia: a candidate who reaches for the hoop value $I=MR^2$ instead of the disc value $I=\frac12 MR^2$ obtains $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+M}=2.45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which is still less than $g$ and so does not look obviously wrong.

provenance.adaptation: Flywheel-and-falling-mass problems are standard in A-level and first-year mechanics, usually stopping at the acceleration. This version keeps the disc and mass values chosen so that a is exactly half of g' in magnitude, adds an explicit energy verification against the rotational share, and introduces a change of regime with a braking torque that requires rotational work. The assembly, the values M = 2.4 kg, R = 0.35 m, m = 0.80 kg, h = 0.90 m and the 0.24 N m brake are all original; every figure was recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Recomputed numerically: a = mg/(m + M/2) = 7.848/2.0 = 3.924 m/s^2; T = Ma/2 = 4.7088 N; v = sqrt(2ah) = 2.6577 m/s; I = 0.1470 kg m^2; omega = 7.5933 rad/s; rotational KE = 4.2379 J; translational KE = 2.8253 J; total = 7.0632 J = mgh. Braking: theta = 4.2379/0.24 = 17.658 rad = 2.8104 revolutions.

questions.title: Two cells in parallel, one of them being charged
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B.5 Current and circuits: emf and internal resistance, epsilon = I(R + r), combinations of resistors in series and parallel, electrical power P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R

questions.question: The diagram shows two cells connected in parallel between the junctions A and B, together with a resistor R of resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ connected between the same two junctions. Cell 1 has emf $\varepsilon_{1}=12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $r_{1}=0.40\ \Omega$; cell 2 has emf $\varepsilon_{2}=9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $r_{2}=0.60\ \Omega$. The connecting wires have negligible resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By applying $\varepsilon=I(R+r)$ to each source branch, and by requiring that the current arriving at junction A equals the current leaving it, show that the potential difference between A and B is $9.64\ \mathrm{V}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in each of the two source branches, stating the direction of each current, and calculate the current in R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the total power delivered by cell 1 equals the sum of the power dissipated in the two internal resistances, the power dissipated in R, and the power absorbed by cell 2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the value of $\varepsilon_{2}$ for which no current flows in branch 2, leaving $\varepsilon_{1}$, $r_{1}$ and $R$ unchanged.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Let $V$ be the potential difference between A and B. In branch 1 the current is $I_{1}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{1}-V}{r_{1}}$ and in branch 2 it is $I_{2}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{2}-V}{r_{2}}$, while the current in R is $I=\dfrac{V}{R}$. **(M1)**

Current is conserved at junction A, so $I_{1}+I_{2}=I$: **(M1)**

$$\frac{12.0-V}{0.40}+\frac{9.0-V}{0.60}=\frac{V}{2.0}$$

Multiplying throughout by $1.2$: $3(12.0-V)+2(9.0-V)=0.6V$. **(M1)**

So $36.0-3V+18.0-2V=0.6V$, giving $54.0=5.6V$ and $V=9.64\ \mathrm{V}$. **(AG)**

**(b)** $I_{1}=\dfrac{12.0-9.643}{0.40}=5.89\ \mathrm{A}$ **(M1)(A1)**, flowing from the positive terminal of cell 1 through junction A and out into the rest of the circuit.

$I_{2}=\dfrac{9.0-9.643}{0.60}=-1.07\ \mathrm{A}$ **(M1)**, so a current of $1.07\ \mathrm{A}$ flows into the positive terminal of cell 2: cell 1 is charging cell 2. **(A1)**

The current in R is $I=\dfrac{9.643}{2.0}=4.82\ \mathrm{A}$. **(A1)**

Check: $5.893-1.071=4.821\ \mathrm{A}$, consistent with current conservation.

**(c)** Power delivered by cell 1: $\varepsilon_{1}I_{1}=12.0\times 5.893=70.7\ \mathrm{W}$. **(M1)**

Power dissipated in the two internal resistances: $I_{1}^{2}r_{1}=5.893^{2}\times 0.40=13.9\ \mathrm{W}$ and $I_{2}^{2}r_{2}=1.071^{2}\times 0.60=0.689\ \mathrm{W}$. **(M1)**

Power dissipated in R: $\dfrac{V^{2}}{R}=\dfrac{9.643^{2}}{2.0}=46.5\ \mathrm{W}$. **(M1)**

Power absorbed by cell 2, which is being charged: $\varepsilon_{2}I_{2}=9.0\times 1.071=9.64\ \mathrm{W}$.

Total $=13.89+0.689+46.49+9.64=70.7\ \mathrm{W}$, which equals the power delivered by cell 1. **(A1)**

**(d)** No current in branch 2 requires $V=\varepsilon_{2}$, since branch 2 then has no potential difference across its internal resistance. **(M1)**

With $I_{2}=0$ the current in branch 1 equals the current in R: $\dfrac{12.0-V}{0.40}=\dfrac{V}{2.0}$, so $2(12.0-V)=0.40V$ and $24.0=2.4V$. **(M1)**

Hence $V=10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $\varepsilon_{2}=10.0\ \mathrm{V}$. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a): the model must include the internal resistances in series with each cell; a candidate who treats the cells as ideal earns at most the second **(M1)**. Accept any consistent choice of sign convention for the current directions, provided it is stated. Part (b): a negative value of $I_{2}$ is the correct outcome and must not be treated as an error; award the **(A1)** for identifying that cell 2 is being charged. A candidate who reverses the direction convention throughout and reports $I_{2}=+1.07\ \mathrm{A}$ into the cell earns full marks if the direction is clearly stated. Part (c): the four power terms are each worth **(M1)**, with the final **(A1)** for demonstrating equality. Follow-through applies from (a) and (b) — if the candidate's currents are consistent with their $V$, the arithmetic will still balance and should be credited. A candidate who omits the power absorbed by cell 2 cannot balance the audit and should not be given the **(A1)**. Part (d): accept a solution by inspection that recognises the no-current condition requires the terminal p.d. of cell 2 to equal its emf.
questions.explanation:
The circuit looks symmetrical and is not. Two cells in parallel with different emfs cannot both deliver current: the potential difference settles between the two emfs, so the stronger cell drives current backwards through the weaker one. Students who assume both cells supply current will set up two positive branch currents, reach a value of $V$ above $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$, and produce an inconsistent current balance without noticing. The sign of $I_{2}$ is the whole point of the question, and part (b) asks for the direction explicitly to make sure it is confronted.

The power audit in part (c) is the strongest check available, and it is worth doing whenever a circuit contains more than one source. Cell 2 absorbs energy at the rate $\varepsilon_{2}I_{2}$ in addition to dissipating $I_{2}^{2}r_{2}$ in its own internal resistance. The two terms are different: the first is energy converted into chemical energy in the cell being charged, the second is energy lost as heat inside it. Omitting the first term is the standard error and it leaves about 14% of the power unaccounted for, which is why the question asks for the audit rather than for a single value.

Part (d) inverts the reasoning. Rather than solving for $V$ given the emfs, it asks what emf would make a branch carry no current, and the answer is that the cell's emf must equal the potential difference across it — the condition for a cell neither charging nor discharging. It is a short part but it tests whether the mechanism behind the terminal potential difference has been understood rather than memorised.

provenance.adaptation: Two-source circuits appear in IB papers but usually with equal emfs or with the sources in series. Here the emfs are chosen so that the weaker cell is unambiguously charged, and the question adds an explicit four-term power audit and an inverse part asking for the emf at which a branch would carry no current. The values, the audit structure and part (d) are original; the node voltage was solved exactly and the power balance verified to six decimal places.

verification.method: Node voltage solved from (12-V)/0.40 + (9-V)/0.60 = V/2.0, giving V = 54/5.6 = 9.6429 V. Branch currents 5.8929 A and -1.0714 A; load current 4.8214 A, and the current balance closes to machine precision. The power audit balances: 70.7143 W delivered equals 13.8903 + 0.6888 + 46.4923 + 9.6429 W.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda=589\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls normally on a double slit. The centres of the two slits are separated by $d=0.400\ \mathrm{mm}$ and each slit has width $b=0.100\ \mathrm{mm}$. The interference pattern is observed on a screen at a distance $D=2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ from the slits. The angles involved are small enough that $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta\approx\theta$ in radians, where convenient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the separation of adjacent bright fringes in the interference pattern.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the centre of the pattern to the first minimum of the single-slit diffraction envelope.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the fourth-order bright fringe is missing from the pattern, and state which other orders would be missing if the screen were large enough to show them.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the number of bright fringes that are visible within the central maximum of the envelope.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The source is replaced by a white light source. Describe one change to the pattern, and explain it.

questions.answer:
**(a)** $s=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}=\dfrac{589\times 10^{-9}\times 2.00}{0.400\times 10^{-3}}$ **(M1)** $=2.94\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}=2.94\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)**

So adjacent bright fringes are $2.94\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. **(A1)**

**(b)** The first minimum of the single-slit envelope is at the smallest angle satisfying $b\sin\theta=\lambda$: **(M1)**

$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}=\dfrac{589\times 10^{-9}}{0.100\times 10^{-3}}=5.89\times 10^{-3}$ **(A1)**

The distance from the centre is $y=D\tan\theta\approx 2.00\times 5.89\times 10^{-3}=1.18\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}=11.8\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)**

**(c)** A double-slit maximum of order $n$ occurs where $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$; the first single-slit minimum occurs where $b\sin\theta=\lambda$. **(M1)**

These coincide when $\dfrac{n\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, that is when $n=\dfrac{d}{b}$. **(M1)**

Here $\dfrac{d}{b}=\dfrac{0.400}{0.100}=4.0$ **(A1)**, so the third-order condition places the minimum at $\theta$ with $\sin\theta=\dfrac{4\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{4\times 589\times 10^{-9}}{0.400\times 10^{-3}}=5.89\times 10^{-3}$, exactly the angle found in part (b). The fourth-order maximum therefore falls on a minimum of the envelope and is not visible. **(A1)**

More generally the missing orders are multiples of $d/b$, so orders $4,\ 8,\ 12,\ \ldots$ are missing. **(A1)** Order 8 would require $\sin\theta=\dfrac{8\lambda}{d}=1.18\times 10^{-2}$, which is still less than $1$, so order 8 is geometrically accessible and would also be missing. Orders beyond the first few visible ones fall outside the envelope's central region anyway.

**(d)** Within the central maximum of the envelope, $\left|\sin\theta\right|<\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so the allowed orders satisfy $\left|n\right|<\dfrac{d}{b}=4$. **(M1)**

So $n=-3,\,-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2,\,3$ are present **(A1)**, giving seven bright fringes. **(A1)** Orders $n=\pm 4$ coincide exactly with the envelope minima from part (c) and are not visible.

**(e)** Each order becomes a continuous spectrum with the same angular spread, with red deviated most because $\theta$ increases with $\lambda$; the central maximum remains white since all wavelengths coincide there and it has no order number. **(A1)(A1)** Higher-order spectra overlap, so beyond the first order the colours are no longer separated cleanly.
questions.markscheme_notes: Parts (a) and (b) are single-formula calculations; accept full marks for any self-consistent use of the small-angle approximation. In (a), the **(A1)** for the unit conversion is separate and should be awarded for 2.94 mm, 2.9 mm or 2.95 mm, but not for 2.94 without a unit. Part (c): the essential reasoning is the equality of the two conditions, not the arithmetic; a candidate who argues from the ratio $d/b$ alone earns **(M1)(M1)(A1)** and the final **(A1)** if the identification of order 4 is complete. Stating that 'all multiples of 4 are missing' without recognising that order 8 is accessible loses the last **(A1)**. Part (d): the mark scheme does not require the exclusion of $n=\pm 4$ to be argued twice, provided the reasoning in (c) is present; a candidate who counts nine fringes has included the two missing orders and can earn at most the first **(M1)**. Part (e): award one mark for a correct change and one for the reason; 'the fringes become coloured' with no reference to wavelength-dependent deviation earns only the first.
questions.explanation:
This question is about two patterns with different length scales occupying the same screen, and about the fact that one of them governs the other. The double-slit fringes are set by $d$; the envelope is set by $b$; and because the two slits have a finite width, the brightness of the fringes is modulated by the diffraction of each individual slit. The envelope is not a curiosity — it determines which fringes exist.

The key step in part (c) is setting the two conditions equal. Because the fringe order is an integer and the ratio $d/b$ is exactly 4, the fourth-order maximum lands precisely on the first envelope minimum. The general result is worth remembering in the form 'orders that are multiples of $d/b$ are missing', and the follow-up question — whether those orders are actually reachable — is what distinguishes a complete answer. With $d/b=4$, order 8 requires $\sin\theta\approx 0.0118$, which is small, so it is reachable and also missing; a student who stops at 'four and eight are missing' without checking is right by luck rather than by reasoning, and the markscheme is written to notice the difference.

Part (d) converts a counting problem into an inequality. The central maximum of the envelope spans $\left|\sin\theta\right|<\lambda/b$, and within it the double-slit maxima satisfy $\left|n\right|<d/b=4$. The integers strictly between $-4$ and $4$ are seven, not nine, because the boundary values are exactly the missing orders. Students who count the boundaries produce nine and have not connected the two parts.

The final part moves from monochromatic light to white light, where each order becomes a spectrum. The central maximum stays white because the path difference is zero for every wavelength simultaneously; every other order is dispersed, with red deviated most. This is the observation that makes a diffraction grating a spectrometer rather than a decoration, and it is worth being able to state in one sentence.

provenance.adaptation: Missing orders in a double-slit pattern are a standard AHL idea, but questions usually ask for the ratio d/b given a missing order, or for the envelope diagram. Here the ratio is fixed at exactly 4 by the chosen geometry, and the question then requires the student to count the surviving fringes inside the envelope and to decide whether the next missing order is geometrically accessible. The values, the counting part and the white-light extension are original; all angles were recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Fringe separation lambda*D/d = 589e-9*2.00/4.00e-4 = 2.945e-3 m. First envelope minimum at sin(theta) = lambda/b = 5.89e-3, giving y = 1.178e-2 m. The ratio d/b = 4.0 exactly, so the fourth-order maximum coincides with the first envelope minimum; the fourth order sits at 4 x 2.945 mm = 11.78 mm, matching the envelope minimum. Orders within the central envelope: |n| < 4.

questions.title: A rod on rails that finds its own terminal speed
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: D.4 Induction (AHL): magnetic flux, Faraday's law, emf induced in a straight conductor moving perpendicular to a field as epsilon = BvL, Lenz's law as a consequence of energy conservation
questions.challenge_mechanism: The rod accelerates until the magnetic force balances the driving force, so the terminal speed has to be found from a force balance rather than from kinematics, and the resulting expression is inversely proportional to the square of both the field and the length, which two separate parts test by different routes that give the same answer.

questions.question: Two long parallel rails, separated by a distance $L=0.60\ \mathrm{m}$, lie in a horizontal plane and are frictionless. A straight conducting rod of mass $m=0.12\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests across the rails and can slide along them. The rails and the rod have negligible resistance, and a resistor of resistance $R=0.80\ \Omega$ connects the rails at one end. Over the whole region between the rails there is a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B=0.45\ \mathrm{T}$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the rails. A light inextensible string attached to the rod passes over a frictionless pulley and supports a hanging mass $m_{2}=0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$. The system is released from rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the rod reaches a terminal speed and derive an expression for that speed in terms of $m_{2}$, $g$, $R$, $B$ and $L$. Calculate its value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that, at the terminal speed, the rate at which the hanging mass loses gravitational potential energy equals the rate at which energy is dissipated in the resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The flux density is doubled to $0.90\ \mathrm{T}$ with everything else unchanged. Determine the new terminal speed and explain why the change is larger than a factor of two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Instead the rod is replaced by a longer rod of the same mass that spans rails a distance $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ apart, with the field restored to $0.45\ \mathrm{T}$. Determine the new terminal speed and explain why it is numerically the same as your answer to part (c).

questions.answer:
**(a)** As the rod accelerates, the emf induced across it is $\varepsilon=BvL$ and the current around the circuit is $I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{BvL}{R}$. The magnetic force opposing the motion is $F=BIL=\dfrac{B^{2}L^{2}v}{R}$. **(M1)(M1)**

For the rod and hanging mass moving together, the resultant driving force is $m_{2}g-F$, so $m_{2}g-\dfrac{B^{2}L^{2}v}{R}=(m+m_{2})a$. **(M1)**

As $v$ increases the opposing force grows, so $a$ falls; when $m_{2}g=\dfrac{B^{2}L^{2}v}{R}$ the acceleration is zero and the speed stops changing. **(A1)**

Hence $v=\dfrac{m_{2}gR}{B^{2}L^{2}}$. **(A1)**

Numerically $v=\dfrac{0.050\times 9.81\times 0.80}{(0.45)^{2}(0.60)^{2}}=\dfrac{0.3924}{0.0729}=5.38\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(A1)**

**(b)** At terminal speed the current is $I=\dfrac{BvL}{R}=\dfrac{0.45\times 5.383\times 0.60}{0.80}=1.82\ \mathrm{A}$. **(M1)**

Power dissipated in the resistor: $I^{2}R=(1.8167)^{2}\times 0.80=2.64\ \mathrm{W}$. **(A1)**

Rate of loss of gravitational potential energy of the hanging mass: $m_{2}gv=0.050\times 9.81\times 5.383=2.64\ \mathrm{W}$, equal to the electrical power. **(A1)** This is the content of Lenz's law: the induced current dissipates energy at exactly the rate at which mechanical energy is supplied, so no energy is created in the circuit.

**(c)** Since $v\propto\dfrac{1}{B^{2}}$, doubling $B$ divides the terminal speed by four: $v=\dfrac{0.3924}{(0.90)^{2}(0.60)^{2}}=\dfrac{0.3924}{0.2916}=1.35\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(M1)(A1)**

The effect is more than a factor of two because the field enters twice. Doubling $B$ doubles the induced emf at a given speed, which on its own would double the current; but that doubled current also experiences twice the magnetic force per ampere. The two doublings compound, so the same retarding force is produced at one quarter of the speed. **(A1)**

**(d)** Since $v\propto\dfrac{1}{L^{2}}$ as well, doubling $L$ again divides the speed by four: $v=\dfrac{0.3924}{(0.45)^{2}(1.20)^{2}}=\dfrac{0.3924}{0.2916}=1.35\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(M1)(A1)**

The two answers agree because $B$ and $L$ appear in the terminal-speed expression only through the product $BL$, which is the quantity that sets both the emf at a given speed and the force at a given current. Doubling either one therefore produces exactly the same change, and the mass of the rod does not enter the expression at all, since at terminal speed the rod's own acceleration is zero. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a): the derivation must include both the emf and the force; a candidate who quotes $F=B^{2}L^{2}v/R$ without showing where it comes from earns one **(M1)** only. The **(A1)** for recognising the terminal condition requires the force balance, not simply 'a is zero'. A candidate who neglects the rod's own mass in the acceleration term still reaches the correct terminal speed, since the masses cancel there; award full marks. Do not accept $v=m_{2}gR/(BL)$ — a confusion between $B$ and $B^{2}$ is a common and costly error that loses the final two marks in (a) and, by follow-through, the marks in (c) and (d) unless the method is otherwise correct. Part (b): the numbers must be compared, not merely asserted; accept $2.6\ \mathrm{W}$ on both sides. Part (c): follow-through applies from (a). The explanation mark requires the double role of B — in the emf and in the force — not just the observation that it is squared. Part (d): credit an answer that notices $BL$ is the only combination that matters. A candidate who tries to include the rod's mass in a momentum argument will not reach 1.35 m/s and should not be given the explanation mark.
questions.explanation:
The rod does not accelerate indefinitely, and the reason is worth stating precisely: the magnetic force is not constant but proportional to the speed. At rest there is no current and no magnetic force, so the driving weight accelerates the system; as the speed rises the induced emf rises, the current rises, and so does the retarding force. Equilibrium is reached when the retarding force equals the driving force, and thereafter the speed is constant even though the hanging mass continues to descend.

The important structural point is that the terminal condition is a force balance, not a statement that the acceleration is zero in some vague sense, and it is reached without solving the differential equation for $v(t)$. This is the same reasoning used for a falling object with air resistance, and recognising the pattern is half the work.

The two final parts are deliberately constructed to produce the same numerical answer by different routes. The expression is $v=m_{2}gR/(B^{2}L^{2})$, so both doubling $B$ and doubling $L$ divide the speed by four, because both quantities enter only through the product $BL$. That product appears once in the emf and once in the force, which is why the square appears. A student who works out that $B$ enters twice but treats $L$ as entering once — for instance by assuming the magnetic force is $BIL$ with $I$ independent of $L$ — will get part (d) wrong and, more importantly, will have missed the structure of the problem.

The mass of the rod never appears in the final answer, which surprises students who expect it to matter. It affects how quickly the terminal speed is reached, not what that speed is, and part (d) makes this concrete by doubling the length while holding the mass fixed.

provenance.adaptation: Rods on rails with a hanging mass are standard in A-level and IB induction problems, but they usually stop at the terminal speed. This version requires the terminal condition to be justified as a force balance, adds an explicit energy audit that doubles as a statement of Lenz's law, and then sets two different changes (doubling B, doubling L) that must give the same answer for a structural reason. The values, the paired parts and the explanation of the BL product are original; every figure was recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Terminal speed from v = m2*g*R/(B^2*L^2). At B = 0.45 T, L = 0.60 m: v = 0.3924/0.0729 = 5.3827 m/s, I = 1.8167 A, I^2 R = 2.6402 W, and m2*g*v = 2.6402 W, confirming the energy balance. Doubling B to 0.90 T gives 0.3924/0.2916 = 1.3457 m/s; doubling L to 1.20 m at 0.45 T gives the same 1.3457 m/s.
